metadata.title: Nothing In It Is Real Yet
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper Development Log, Week 13 — Phase 3 opens with a decoupled React dashboard for compliance reviewers: why it replaces the Week 5 template dashboard, the three operational layers, the mock telemetry contract it runs on, and why a provenance tool displaying invented numbers has to say so out loud.

metadata.audience: Humanitarians AI fellows following the Provenance Gatekeeper build
metadata.source: Week 13: Building the React Monitoring Dashboard — 5-scene script, supplied 2026-11-26.
metadata.dual_render: 16:9 master + 9:16 companion. Every pattern has a registered <Pattern>916 variant. ZERO new components. Built straight to ./art final — no review cut, so no beat chip or timecode is ever drawn and GATE V runs on both aspects.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude FIDELITY skin — cream #FAF9F5 / stage #F2F0E9, warm ink #3D3929, terracotta #D97757 as the ONE accent. The script describes a DARK-MODE dashboard; it renders here in the Claude skin as labelled wireframe panels. Intent preserved, not the hex values — the same ruling made for this series' palette in Week 2.
metadata.channel_note: Narrated in the FIRST PERSON by Onkar Bhujbal. Kokoro am_onyx is a synthetic read of Onkar's own script, not a clone of his voice.
metadata.series_note: OVERLAP: Week 5 (claude-gatekeeper-dashboard-stress, 'Expose The Ledger') already built a dashboard over this same ledger and already argued human fatigue, closing on 'a ledger nobody opens is a ledger nobody has.' This reel does NOT repeat that argument. It justifies the second dashboard on two grounds the script itself gives — decoupling from FastAPI, and a non-engineer audience — and spends its added beat on what is genuinely new and uncomfortable: the thing is wired to mock data.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. Over twelve weeks this thing has grown a vector store, token authentication, an alert pipeline, a Redis cache and Prometheus telemetry. And the person who most needs to trust it — a compliance officer — cannot read any of it. Raw JSON and PromQL are not an interface for them. This week opens Phase three: a React monitoring dashboard built for the human who has to sign off.

beats.authoring_note: Both readings are true sentences: 'The dashboard is live.' and, corrected, 'The dashboard is drawn.' The correction is the honest one and the second line holds for either.

beats.narration_text: Fair question: I built a dashboard in Week five. That one was an H.T.M.L. template served by FastAPI — welded to the inference service, so every styling change redeployed the verifier. This time the frontend is a separate React and Vite app that talks to the backend over H.T.T.P. and knows nothing else about it.

beats.authoring_note: The script does not mention the Week 5 dashboard. Naming it is an editorial addition — a second dashboard over the same ledger needs a reason, and the script supplies two (decoupling, non-engineer audience). Ignoring the first one would look like the series forgot it.

beats.narration_text: The layout is three operational layers. Across the top, K.P.I. cards — claims evaluated, hallucinations blocked, cache hit rate, average latency. Beneath that, an infrastructure strip showing all five containers, so a reviewer can tell at a glance whether they are looking at a quiet day or a dead pipeline — which, as I said last week, render identically. And filling the rest of the screen, the intercepted payload ledger.

beats.authoring_note: The 'quiet day or dead pipeline' line deliberately calls back to Week 12's falsifiability beat, where a flat line and a dead exporter were shown to render identically. The infra strip is the UI answer to that problem.

beats.act: SCENE 4 — THE LEDGER AND ITS CONTRACT
beats.narration_text: The centrepiece is the intercepted hallucination ledger. A reviewer filters by variance type and sees the fabricated claim beside the ChromaDB ground truth — the one layout that makes a judgement possible. Underneath is a strict mock telemetry contract: the exact shape next week's authenticated endpoints must return, so the swap is a data source change, not a rewrite.
beats.new_visual_element: The shape the real endpoint has to match

show.event: code card opens on a hard cut; traffic-light dot arms terracotta
the row shape reveals — claim beside ground truth
the filter keys reveal
the closing note lands: next week this import changes, nothing else

props.title: data/mockTelemetry.js
props.sparkLine: Design the contract, then fill it.

beats.honesty_note: Every value in this object is fabricated for the mock. That is the point of B05. The row shape reflects what the ledger would need to carry for a reviewer to adjudicate a claim.

beats.narration_text: Now the part I want to be careful about. Everything on this dashboard is invented — the blocked counts, the cache hit rate, the claims in the ledger. I wrote them. And a dashboard is a format that confers authority: four figures in cards, a green row of containers, and it reads as a report whether or not anything behind it is connected. For a system built to catch fabricated numbers, shipping an interface full of fabricated numbers is the exact failure mode wearing my own design. So until it is bound to live endpoints it carries a banner, and a screenshot of it is not evidence.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED, and it is the reel's reason to exist. The script mentions the mock contract once, in Scene 4, framed as forward planning. Building the contract first IS good practice and the reel says so — but a provenance tool rendering invented figures in an authoritative format is the project's own failure mode pointed at itself, and that deserves to be said out loud rather than discovered by a viewer who screenshots it.

beats.narration_text: So design the interface for the human reviewer — great backend architecture is worth nothing if the person accountable cannot see what it caught. And while your data is mocked, make the interface admit it, in a way nobody can crop out.

beats.authoring_note: Deriving the banner from the data source rather than an environment flag is the reel's addition — a flag is exactly the thing that gets left wrong in a demo build.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own interface. Ask a model which numbers on your dashboard a reader would assume are live, and which of those could currently be stale, cached, mocked or partially loaded without the interface showing any difference. Every one it finds is a place your U.I. is making a promise your data is not keeping.
